opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say the main novelty is less about one single trick and more about how we combined the pieces so that the model sounds natural while staying practical to run.

The core idea is to treat speech generation as a language modeling problem over audio tokens, building on the backbone work we'd already done on the text and speech-understanding side. Voxtral started as a speech-understanding model, so we already had a strong audio representation and a lot of experience aligning audio with text. With TTS we're essentially running that in the other direction: the model has to produce audio rather than just consume it.

The hard part, and where most of the effort went, is the audio representation itself. If your tokenizer is too lossy, you get that slightly robotic, flattened prosody. If it's too fine-grained, sequences get very long, generation is slow, and the model struggles with long-range consistency. So a lot of the work was on getting a codec that preserves expressiveness, things like intonation, pauses, and speaker identity, while keeping the token rate low enough that you can generate in real time.

The second piece is voice adaptation. We wanted the model to pick up a speaker's characteristics from a short reference clip and keep that voice stable over a long generation, including across languages. Getting cross-lingual consistency right, where the same voice speaks French or Spanish and still sounds like the same person, was something we cared a lot about given that we're a European company with very multilingual users.

And then there's the practical side: latency and streaming. For voice agents, you need the first audio out very quickly, so the architecture was designed with streaming in mind rather than as an afterthought.

So if I had to summarize: it's a unified approach where understanding and generation share a lot of the same foundations, with a big focus on the audio tokenization and on making it fast and multilingual enough to actually be used in production.

r001.rationale: The response describes speech generation as language modeling over audio tokens but does not identify autoregressive flow matching as the architecture.

r002.rationale: It discusses keeping the codec token rate low, but gives no rate of 1.5 Hz.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the main thing we tried to do with Voxtral TTS is to stop treating speech generation as a separate pipeline bolted onto a language model, and instead treat it as a native output modality of the same decoder.

So concretely, the model is a single autoregressive transformer that operates over interleaved text tokens and acoustic tokens. The acoustic side comes from a neural codec we trained ourselves, with a fairly low frame rate and a small number of codebooks, because we found that most of the quality loss in TTS systems was not in the language model but in the tokenizer. If your codec throws away prosody, there is nothing the LM can do to recover it. So a lot of the work was on getting a codec that preserves speaker identity, intonation, and timing at a low bitrate, so that the sequence the transformer has to model stays short.

The second piece is that we don't predict the codebooks in a slow, hierarchical way where you need many forward passes per frame. We use a delayed pattern across codebooks so that one step of the big model produces a full frame, and a very small local transformer handles the residual codebooks. That is what lets us run at well below real time on a single GPU, which matters a lot for the use cases people actually have, like voice agents, where latency to first audio is the whole product.

And the third thing, which I think is the more interesting one from a research point of view, is that because it shares the backbone with our speech understanding models, the model has a real understanding of the text it is reading. So it handles things like numbers, abbreviations, code-switching between languages mid-sentence, and the kind of emphasis you would expect from context, without any explicit front-end normalization. We spent a lot of effort on multilingual data, especially European languages, where most existing TTS systems degrade quite a bit.

So if I had to summarize, the novelty is less one trick and more the combination: a good low-rate codec, an efficient decoding pattern that gives low latency, and a language model that actually understands what it is saying.

r001.rationale: The response describes a single autoregressive transformer over text and acoustic tokens, but does not identify autoregressive flow matching as the architecture.

r002.rationale: It says the codec has a low frame rate, but gives no rate of 1.5 Hz.

sol-6.1.text: I’d frame the novelty around streaming. It’s not just about generating a convincing voice; it’s about producing speech before you have the entire utterance, while keeping the prosody coherent. Those goals are in tension: more context helps you decide how a sentence should sound, but waiting for that context adds latency. The interesting technical question is how you manage that tradeoff while preserving naturalness and speaker identity.
